content.text:
Nature and science facts about stag beetles

A stag beetle's magnificent pincers are actually its greatly enlarged jaws (mostly on males). Over a good spot where tree sap flows well, males have pushing contests with their pincers against other males (pushing each other away rather than injuring). They go through a complete transformation (egg → larva → pupa → adult), and the larva grows for a long time inside rotting wood, feeding on that wood. Beneath its hard outer wings, it keeps its flying wings folded, then spreads them to fly.

Parent guide — how to nurture curiosity

Tell your child "The pincers are actually jaws" and compare them to a rhinoceros beetle (which has a horn). Observing insects on a sap-oozing oak tree on a summer night makes it even more exciting.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. What are a stag beetle's pincers?
A. They're actually greatly enlarged jaws. Mostly males have them, and they use them for pushing contests over sap spots.

Q. What do the larvae eat?
A. They grow for a long time inside rotting wood, feeding on that wood. They go through a complete transformation.

Q. How can we observe them at home?
A. Learn that "pincers = jaws," compare them with a rhinoceros beetle, and watch for sap on oak trees on summer nights.
